questions.stem: Two branch routers protect traffic between their LANs across the internet, and the original packets' internal addresses must not be visible in transit. Which IPsec choice BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: the whole original packet, headers included, is encapsulated and encrypted.
Encrypts the payload but leaves the original IP header visible.
AH doesn't encrypt, so the inner addresses stay readable.
Neither hides headers nor encrypts.

questions.explanation: ESP uses symmetric ciphers (AES preferred), with keys negotiated via IKE using Diffie-Hellman. Tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet (site-to-site); transport mode protects the payload only.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tunnel = whole packet encapsulated; transport = payload only.

questions.stem: An analyst on the internet path between two sites captures the packet below. What BEST describes the tunnel?

options.text: It carries multicast, but nothing is encrypted
options.rationale: Correct: the OSPF hello inside is plainly readable.

options.text: It is a GRE tunnel between the two sites
options.rationale: True, but it misses the security point: no encryption.

options.text: It is an IPsec tunnel using ESP
options.rationale: ESP would hide the inner packet.

options.text: It encrypts the OSPF hello inside
options.rationale: The capture shows the hello in the clear.

questions.explanation: GRE (IP protocol 47) is encapsulation that can carry many protocols, including multicast and routing protocols. It is flexible but provides no encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: GRE is flexible but provides no encryption.

questions.stem: Two sites must run OSPF between them across the internet, and their traffic must be encrypted. Which option BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: GRE carries the multicast routing traffic; IPsec encrypts it.
Carries OSPF, but without encryption.

options.text: An IPsec crypto map without GRE
options.rationale: A policy-based crypto map doesn't carry OSPF's multicast.

options.text: An SSL VPN for each user
options.rationale: User VPNs don't link the sites' routers.

questions.explanation: GRE over IPsec protects a GRE tunnel with IPsec: GRE adds multiprotocol and multicast support, such as routing protocols, and IPsec adds encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: GRE adds multicast support; IPsec adds encryption.

questions.stem: A retailer has one hub and 300 stores. Stores sometimes need to exchange traffic directly, and configuring a full mesh of tunnels by hand isn't feasible. Which design BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: spokes build direct tunnels on demand, with no full mesh to configure.

options.text: Hub-and-spoke IPsec with no spoke links
options.rationale: Works, but store-to-store traffic always detours through the hub.

options.text: A full mesh of static IPsec tunnels
options.rationale: Tens of thousands of tunnels to configure by hand.

options.text: An SSL VPN for each store manager
options.rationale: Remote-access VPNs don't connect store networks.

questions.explanation: Cisco DMVPN is a hub-and-spoke VPN with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels, built from mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec. It scales without configuring a full mesh.
questions.discriminator_tested: DMVPN scales without configuring a full mesh.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a Cisco IPsec VTI from a crypto-map-based tunnel?

options.rationale: Correct: route-based IPsec on a virtual interface.

options.text: It is configured on Cisco routers
options.rationale: True of both, so it doesn't distinguish them.

options.text: It adds a GRE header to carry multicast
options.rationale: That describes GRE over IPsec.

options.text: It builds tunnels between spokes on demand
options.rationale: That describes DMVPN.

questions.explanation: A Cisco IPsec VTI is an IPsec tunnel presented as a routable virtual interface: route-based, with no GRE header. Crypto maps are policy-based.

questions.stem: A company sets up an internal CA, certificate templates, issuance and revocation policies, and automatic enrollment for its laptops. What BEST describes what it has built?

options.rationale: Correct: the whole trust system.
One component of what was built.
Templates are one part.
PKI is built on public/private key pairs.

questions.explanation: Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the framework of CAs, certificates, policies, and processes that bind public keys to identities. It is the whole trust system, not one component.
questions.discriminator_tested: PKI is the whole trust system.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why a certificate authority is the trust anchor in a PKI?

options.text: It signs with its private key
options.rationale: Correct: anyone trusting the CA can verify its signature.

options.text: It issues certificates to users and devices
options.rationale: True, but issuing alone wouldn't create trust without the signature.

options.text: It stores users' private keys for recovery
options.rationale: A CA signs public keys; it doesn't normally hold users' private keys.
Hosts encrypt their own traffic.

questions.explanation: Certificate authorities are trusted entities that issue, sign, and revoke certificates. A CA is the trust anchor because it signs with its own private key.
questions.discriminator_tested: The CA signs with its own private key.

questions.stem: An administrator changes a certificate template's validity period from two years to one. Which certificates does this change MOST directly affect?

options.rationale: Correct: a template is the blueprint for future issuance.

options.text: Certificates issued for that template's purpose
options.rationale: Too vague; existing ones keep their original dates.
Issued certificates keep the dates they were signed with.
The CA certificate isn't issued from that template.

questions.explanation: A certificate template is the predefined settings (key usage, validity, key size, subject fields) a CA applies when issuing certificates. It is the blueprint for issuance, not a certificate itself.
questions.discriminator_tested: A template is the blueprint for issuance, not a certificate.

questions.stem: A colleague plans to back up the certificate shown below so the server's TLS identity can be restored on new hardware. What BEST explains why the certificate alone isn't enough?
questions.exhibit:
Subject:     CN=portal.example.com
Issuer:      CN=Example Issuing CA
Valid:       2025-11-01 to 2026-11-01
Public key:  RSA (2048 bits)
Key usage:   Digital Signature, Key Encipherment

options.text: It has no copy of the private key
options.rationale: Correct: the private key must be backed up separately and securely.

options.text: It is signed by the issuing CA, not the server
options.rationale: True, but irrelevant to restoring the server's identity.

options.text: It expires in a year and must be renewed
options.rationale: Expiry is a separate issue.

options.text: It is encrypted with the CA's private key
options.rationale: The CA signs it; the certificate isn't encrypted.

questions.explanation: Certificates are signed documents binding a public key to an identity (X.509). They hold the public key, never the private key, and are validated by the CA's signature, their dates, and their revocation status.
questions.discriminator_tested: A certificate holds the public key, never the private key.

questions.stem: Which command creates a standard ACL entry that permits the 192.168.1.0/24 network?

options.rationale: Correct: number, action, source, and wildcard.
A subnet mask where a wildcard belongs.
110 is an extended number, which requires a protocol.
Standard ACLs take no protocol.

questions.explanation: Standard ACL commands are entered in global config, such as 'access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255': a number, an action, and a source plus wildcard, with no protocol or ports.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard: number, action, source plus wildcard; no protocol or ports.

questions.stem: Which extended ACL entry permits web traffic from 10.1.4.0/24 to server 10.1.9.10?

options.rationale: Correct: action, protocol, source, destination, port.
Source and destination are reversed.
'ip' can't take a port.
The action must come before the protocol.

questions.explanation: Extended ACL commands follow the order action, protocol, source, destination, then port, as in 'access-list 110 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.10 eq 80'.
questions.discriminator_tested: Order is action, protocol, source, destination, port.

questions.stem: The router rejects the commands below. What BEST explains why?
questions.exhibit:
R1(config)# ip access-list WEB-IN
% Incomplete command.
R1(config)# permit tcp any any eq 443
% Invalid input detected at '^' marker.

options.text: The 'extended' keyword is missing from the first line
options.rationale: Correct: named ACLs need 'standard' or 'extended'.

options.text: The entry was typed in the wrong mode
options.rationale: A consequence: the first line failed, so the router never entered ACL config mode.

options.text: Named ACL entries must start with 'access-list'
options.rationale: Named ACL entries omit the 'access-list' keyword.

options.text: Named ACLs don't accept port numbers
options.rationale: Extended named ACLs accept ports.

questions.explanation: Named ACLs start with 'ip access-list extended NAME' (or 'standard'), then take entries such as 'permit tcp any any eq 443' in ACL config mode. The keyword is required, and entries omit 'access-list'.

questions.stem: After the configuration below, Telnet to 10.1.9.10 still works. What is the MOST likely reason?
questions.exhibit:
access-list 110 deny tcp any host 10.1.9.10 eq 23
access-list 110 permit ip any any
!
interface g0/1
 description To server LAN

options.text: ACL 110 was never applied to an interface
options.rationale: Correct: an unapplied ACL filters nothing.

options.text: The final 'permit ip any any' overrides the deny
options.rationale: First match wins, so the deny would match first.
Telnet runs over TCP 23.

options.text: The deny entry should come after the permit
options.rationale: Then the permit would match first and allow Telnet.

questions.explanation: An ACL is applied with 'ip access-group 110 in' (or out) under the interface. An unapplied ACL filters nothing; direction is relative to the router, and there is one ACL per protocol, interface, and direction.

questions.stem: Just the admin subnet 10.1.9.0/24 may open SSH sessions to the router, and ACL 10 already permits that subnet. Which command completes the job?

options.rationale: Correct: limits management sessions to the device.

options.text: ip access-group 10 in, under interface g0/0
options.rationale: That filters traffic passing through the interface.
'out' restricts sessions from the router, not to it.
Sets authentication; doesn't restrict sources.

questions.explanation: Applying an ACL to VTY lines uses 'line vty 0 4' then 'access-class 10 in'. access-class limits management sessions to the device; ip access-group filters traffic through an interface.
questions.discriminator_tested: access-class limits sessions to the device; access-group filters through traffic.

questions.stem: Host 10.1.4.66 can still SSH anywhere despite the ACL shown below. What is the BEST fix?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show access-lists BRANCH
Extended IP access list BRANCH
    10 permit ip 10.1.4.0 0.0.0.255 any (812 matches)
    20 deny tcp host 10.1.4.66 any eq 22

options.rationale: Correct: the specific entry must come before the broad one.

options.text: Add the deny again at the end of the list
options.rationale: It would still sit below entry 10 and never match.
Still shadowed by entry 10.

options.text: Remove the ACL from the interface
options.rationale: That removes all filtering.

questions.explanation: New numbered entries append to the end; sequence numbers let you insert or delete entries in named ACLs. A broad entry above a specific one shadows it, and entry 20 shows no matches for that reason.
questions.discriminator_tested: A broad entry above a specific one shadows it.

questions.stem: Which two ACL entries will the router reject? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: 'ip' matches all traffic and can't take ports.
Correct: ICMP takes message types, not port operators.
Valid: ports require tcp or udp.
Valid: 'range' works with udp.

options.text: permit tcp any any eq www
options.rationale: Valid: port names are accepted.

questions.explanation: Port and protocol keywords: protocols tcp, udp, icmp, ip; operators eq, neq, gt, lt, range; ports by name or number. Ports require tcp or udp; 'ip' matches all traffic and can't take ports.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ports require tcp or udp; 'ip' can't take ports.

questions.stem: An engineer needs to confirm which ACL is applied to interface g0/0 and in which direction. Which command BEST shows that?

options.rationale: Correct: it lists the inbound and outbound ACLs on that interface.
Would show it among everything else, but less directly.
Shows the ACL's entries and hits, not where it is applied.
Shows routing, not filtering.

questions.explanation: When verifying ACLs, 'show access-lists' shows what the ACL says and its hits; 'show ip interface' shows where it is applied and in which direction.
questions.discriminator_tested: show access-lists = contents and hits; show ip interface = where applied.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes the difference between 'no ip access-group 110 in' on an interface and 'no access-list 110' in global config?

options.text: The first unapplies the ACL; the second deletes it
options.rationale: Correct: application vs the ACL itself.

options.text: The first deletes the ACL; the second unapplies it
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Both stop ACL 110 filtering on that interface
options.rationale: True, but the second also deletes the ACL everywhere.

options.text: Both delete entry 110 alone from the list
options.rationale: 110 is the ACL number, not an entry.

questions.explanation: 'no ip access-group 110 in' removes only the application; 'no access-list 110' deletes the whole ACL. 'remark' documents an entry.
questions.discriminator_tested: Removing the application vs deleting the ACL.
